title: The world outside, first grey shapes, and what the openings really frame (work in progress)

media.caption: The outside as plain grey shapes, seen from above and from two sides: the rift on the sunrise side, broken walls and a tower on the sunset side, a young crater with a lake in a ring of dead trees, an old crater, terraces, dunes far off. The sculpture is the white shape in the middle. Exposure lowered about seven times so the shapes show (not physical): at the cave's true exposure the open daylight turns white.
Looking out through the 20 largest openings, from inside. They show black: the sky is not drawn yet. None of them shows the grey land, because they point up.

notes: Work in progress: placeholder shapes, nothing final.

What this changes: the sky is most of the outside world a visitor sees. It comes first (the live sky, the anti-sun, moons and stars), then tall things that rise into the openings' view (cliffs, towers, giant trees, plumes), then the ground.
The sky is not drawn yet; through the openings it is black. The white seen in openings until now was the sculpture's own sunlit outer skin.
Open question: open daylight is far brighter than the cave, and the display turns it white. Glare as a mood, a gentler curve for what is seen through openings, or a hazier, dimmer outside.
Method: own measurement (rays leaving the cave from 1,858 head positions).

media.caption: Left: the share of the sculpture's surface a visitor can ever see from inside, as published on October 11 and corrected now. Right: the visible surface by how close a visitor can get to it.

notes: About 58 % of the sculpture's surface (241 of 412 square metres) can ever be seen from inside, and 105 square metres of it from closer than 25 cm.

Correction: the October 11 figure (about 80 % seen, 182 square metres closer than 25 cm) counted head positions just outside the walls, under the sculpture's overhang, so it included the outer skin. The toad is now one skin: body, head, glands, warts and legs melt into each other, so the legs bend at the joints instead of coming apart when it hops.

Still open (from a fresh review): the eyes still sit a little proud like knobs, it stands too tall on its legs, the fingers are too long and thin, and it casts no shadow on the stone yet.

Flies and gnats are now in the cave as the toad's prey. Flies bask on lit stone and dart off from a hand; gnats hover over damp shade. The toad misses about 4 strikes in 10 (art-directed: Samuel wanted it a little clumsy).

title: A world outside the sculpture: proposal (awaiting Samuel)

media.caption: Looking around from the middle of the cave. Top row standing, bottom row lying on the floor; the last picture of each row looks straight up. The white patches are the outside, seen through the openings.
How much of the view shows the outside, measured from 14 places in the cave. Lying or crouching, about 1 %, mostly overhead; standing, 3 to 6 %, in every direction.

notes: Proposal, nothing built yet.
Because the outside is only seen in small framed glimpses, it would be built as windows: a small scene placed where each opening looks, things crossing the sky, and a far horizon behind them.
Windows (2 to 15 m): real shapes lit by the same live sun and sky as the cave, built only where an opening looks. They must hold up close, because visitors lean into the openings.
Sky: things that cross it, such as birds, dust devils, heat shimmer and plumes. Lying visitors see it most.
Far horizon: a 360 picture or short loop, made by us from a real 3D landscape at several sun positions, so it follows the day.

The story: old ruined ground that the earth is still tearing apart. A rift where the plates split, breathing hot air and wind that colour the sky. Broken walls and stairs to nowhere where birds perch, two craters (one with a still pool that mirrors the sky), desert scrub, a dead tree, dunes, large animals far off, and a few impossible things, such as rocks hovering in the hot updraft or a mirage lake that is never there when you lean closer.

Samuel's direction (Oct 13): fantastical, a little dangerous, but something really nice about it; a whole ecology with 20 to 50 % strangeness, never corny alien; geology that follows rules, continuing the ruin floor with softer parts; the rift's winds mostly in the sound and the sky (colouring it, a violent eruption can stir the dust inside), not the main cause of the wind; the outside will catch the low, almost level sun and block some of it, giving the light inside more of a story. A soundscape will follow it.
Method: own measurement (126 views from 14 positions inside the cave, the outside isolated by switching off the direct sun).

title: Replacing Unity and Octane: our own engine, two days in

media.caption: The breathing walls in the afternoon sun, without rain. The strands sway and the walls slowly swell; their shadows move with them, each strand brightens as it turns toward the sun, the light bounced from the rest of the cave shifts as they turn, and the thinnest strands glow where the sun is behind them. Breathing amplitude and the strength of the glow are art-directed.
The permanent pool between storms: slow drips fall from the rock, each sending a ring across the still water, which reflects the live sky through the openings.
Light at the walls, left: one bake; right: eight independent bakes averaged and smoothed on the surface by a filter fitted to how they disagree (brightened to show the grain).

notes: Gloam is replacing both Unity, the game engine it played in, and Octane, the renderer that baked its light, with a player and a light engine we wrote ourselves. This post shows what that bought, in numbers, what we built on top of it today, and the plan ahead, including the strange parts.

Why leave Unity and Octane. Gloam's day of light is about 16,000 baked 8K lightmaps that stream to the VR display while a visitor walks. In Unity every lightmap swap froze the program for 80 to 95 milliseconds. At 90 frames a second a frame lasts 11 milliseconds, so each swap dropped seven or eight frames, and in VR a dropped frame is felt in the stomach, not just seen.

Unity against our player. One 8K lightmap upload: 80 to 95 milliseconds in Unity, during which nothing moved; 5.7 in our player, done on the side while the picture keeps moving. Light changes per second without a dropped frame: about 2 in Unity; 5.3 in our player, with no frame over the 11 millisecond budget. Re-lighting the whole sculpture: about a year of Octane renders; now live light from the sky and sun, and the light at every point rebakes in about 15 minutes. Sculpture drawn per frame: everything in Unity; in our player only what can be seen from where you stand (about a quarter of the pieces at a time).

Today's gains on top of that, each measured before and after on the same view. Drawing only what can be seen: the graphics card's time per frame went from 4.8 to 3.4 milliseconds. Storing the light more compactly: 350 MB down to 186 MB. Playing back the rain on the sculpture: 8.9 milliseconds of computer time per frame with frames dropped, now 0.16 with none dropped. Storm data on disk (a 30 second sample): 2.2 GB down to 1.0 GB.

What we built today. Vivarium, our own file format (private for now): the artwork as one package of layers (shape, light, motion, visibility, water, growth), each checked against the shape it belongs to, so a stale piece is refused instead of drawing wrong.
The sculpture in small clusters, loaded by what you can see: light and motion now live per cluster in a shared pool that follows the visitor; the same machinery carries storms and, later, growth.
Rain as time pages: a storm is stored per piece of the sculpture and per second, only where water actually is; the computer no longer rebuilds the wetness of 3.7 million points every frame.
One clock for time of day, storms and exhibition days, and a growth layer that will remember what grew and wore away across the days of an exhibition.

The breathing walls now carry their own light: their shadows move with them, each strand brightens as it leans toward the sun, and the light bounced around the cave shifts as each strand turns: every point of the wall knows, from its own place in the fur, how its light changes when it leans. Where the sun is behind them, the thinnest strands glow through.

Smoother light without waiting longer: the light is baked several times independently and the engine learns, from how those bakes disagree, how much to smooth it on the surface itself, keeping the fine shading of the fur and removing the grain.

A permanent pool at the back, holding water between storms and reflecting the live sky. Plants that need soil: grass and flowers only where old cracks have filled with sediment, nothing under the drips or in the pool.
Two independent reviews of the engine work (by another AI model), and every serious finding fixed; then a cleanup that removed duplicated code without changing a pixel.

The plan ahead, near: the floor as an ancient ruin, broken over aeons: split, tilted and sunken stones, soil under some of them, wide joints filled with moss and grit. Small life: snails, woodlice, springtails, toads; then curious squirrels and birds that come to look at you, let you near if you move slowly, and fly off if you move too fast. Sound: birds near and far, wings, drips, wind. Your own hands in the space, and later your body. The rain again, now on the new engine, still changing the light.

Further, and stranger (ideas, not built). White holes: columns where water, or smoke, or something with no name, pours endlessly from nowhere: the calm of a waterfall or a fire. Will-o'-the-wisps: pale green and blue flames that rise at night, the cold glow that marsh gases were once seen to give off. Comets crossing the night sky so brightly they light the cave, and scare the birds into flight, wings beating, screaming.
Offline renders, made frame by frame; not something you can walk through.

Sources: our own measurements on the same workstation and the same views before and after each change (frame times over hundreds of frames, upload times, file sizes); the two engine reviews' reports. Marsh lights: the slow burning of marsh gases (methane, with traces of phosphine) is the usual explanation, though it has never been fully confirmed.

title: Rejected, being reworked: the floor as an old ruin (first attempt)
notes: Rejected by Samuel and being reworked: he found it "a mush of stuff. Not the floor of an old ruin". Kept here as a record of the first attempt.

Samuel asked for a floor that looks like a really old ruin, broken over ages: "it's not paving anymore, it's a ruin". Each stone has split into several pieces. About half of the pieces came loose and settled on their own, tilted, raised or sunk by up to about 2 cm, so the edges no longer meet, and some pieces are gone, with soil where they were. The gaps have widened to 1 to 3 cm and filled with soil and grit, and the edges are worn round. Some stones have lost a flake off one side.

Where water stands on a flat stone, shallow solution pans form; under the drips the stone has dissolved into cups about 2 cm deep. Limestone wears down by roughly 0.035 to 0.4 mm a year depending on exposure, so cups of a few centimetres fit a couple of thousand years under a drip.

Soil also lies under about a third of the stones, more where it is damp and sheltered. Plants root in the gaps, where pieces are missing, and along the edges of stones with soil under them, never on bare stone tops. Dark lichen crusts grow on the shaded stone.

Art-directed, not measured: the size of the pieces, how many came loose or are gone, how far they moved, how wide the gaps are, the rounding of the edges, and where the soil lies. The pool stays where it was; its water level is measured from the new ground.
One limit: the ground's shape is held on a 1 cm grid, so details smaller than that (fine pitting, small chips) are not in its shape. Small chips will come as real separate stones.
Offline renders, made frame by frame; not something you can walk through.

Sources: solution pans (kamenitzas) in the karren literature (Cucchi 2009, Karst Rock Features); limestone surface lowering measured with micro-erosion meters (St Paul's Cathedral, London; Adriatic shore studies); dark crustose lichen spectra (Greenland lichens); plant communities by soil depth on rock outcrops.

media.caption: The floor as an old ruin (left: before; right: after): stones split, shifted and partly gone, wide gaps filled with soil, plants rooting from the gaps and from under some stones. Seen from above near a flower.
The usual crouching view, before (left) and as a ruin (right).
The pool, before (left) and on the ruin floor (right). The pool keeps its place and its still water.

superseded_note: Samuel found it a mush of soft lumps, not an old ruin. The rework gives each stone a flat, worn top with its own tilt, crisp edges, dark soil-filled joints with the plants in them, pale stone against dark soil, and stones cracked, lifted or missing.

title: Plants only where the soil is deep enough; why the pool looks dark from above
notes: Plants on rock sort themselves by how much soil they have. Moss and lichen need none and live on bare stone. Small flowering plants need about 2.5 cm or more, and grasses about 18 cm or more (studies of plants on rock outcrops). The floor now follows this: the old cracks between the stones have filled with sediment over a long time, and plants grow only where a crack holds enough soil for them. Nothing roots on bare stone, under the drips (the soil is washed out) or in the pool.

How deep the cracks are is art-directed, not measured: about 40 cm at the widest, Samuel's call for old, deep cracks full of sediment. With that, the widest and wettest cracks carry grass and the narrow ones only flowers and moss.

Why the pool looks dark from above: looking straight down, still water reflects only about 2 % of the light, so you mostly see its wet floor. The pale shapes on it are the bright openings overhead reflected: even 2 % of them outshines the shaded stone. Toward grazing angles the surface becomes almost a mirror.
Next: the floor becomes an old ruin, its stones split, tilted, worn and partly gone, with soil under some of them.
Offline renders, made frame by frame; not something you can walk through.

Sources: plant communities by soil depth on rock outcrops (New Georgia Encyclopedia, granite outcrops; University of Salamanca pasture study); JNCC limestone pavement account (crack depths); Fresnel reflection of water (2 % at normal incidence).

media.caption: Crouching view, before and after the soil rule: plants grow only where the old, sediment-filled cracks hold enough soil (about 40 cm deep at the widest, art-directed), never on bare stone, under the drips or in the pool.
A flower spot from above, with the permanent pool at the top left. 14 flowers root in crack soil; 7 spots with no soil nearby stay bare.

The permanent pool, which no longer empties between storms. Seen from above, water reflects only about 2 % of the light, so the pool reads dark and you see its wet floor. The pale shapes are reflections of the bright openings overhead. Toward grazing angles the surface becomes almost a mirror.

title: The pool keeps its water, plants only where there is soil
notes: Samuel's review of the first pass: the empty pool looked wrong, grass and flowers still grew on dry stone, and the small dark ovals painted on the floor read as lenses, not pebbles.

The pool now always holds water. Over years, fine silt carried in by muddy run-off clogs the pores of a rock pool's floor, so it stops leaking and stays full between storms, drawn down only by evaporation. It rests half a centimetre below the point where it would spill over, and covers about 0.37 square metres, up to 12 cm deep (about 21 litres). The still surface mirrors the cave: the bright openings in the rock above show in it, and the stone at its bottom looks wet. The rain simulation now starts with the pool full and its floor sealed, so storms raise it toward the rim rather than filling an empty hollow.

Plants need soil. On a floor of slabs like this, soil only collects in the cracks between them, as on limestone pavement, where the cracks hold the plants and the slab tops stay bare or crusted. The flowers and the grass around them now root only in cracks, never under the drips (the soil is washed out there) or in the pool. Where a flower had no crack near its spot, it is gone: 11 flowers remain and 4 were removed.
The painted pebbles are gone. Pebbles will come back as real stones with their own shape, lit like everything else, never painted onto the ground.
The zone map now has a legend. The black shapes are the sculpture's pillars and walls standing in the room, where there is no floor.
Cost: crouched right over the pool, with the water filling the view, drawing it adds about 0.3 milliseconds per frame (3.6 instead of 3.3 on that view, on the workstation).
Not yet: the water bends the view of the bottom (refraction), muddy water after rain that clears as it settles, a high-water line, and soil deep enough for each kind of plant.
Offline renders, made frame by frame; not something you can walk through.

Sources: colmation (pores clogged by fine sediment) in the SedNet studies and column experiments; Natural England and JNCC accounts of limestone pavement; studies of crack-dwelling plants (Schimper; Davis 1982); Lekner and Dorf 1988 on why wet surfaces look darker; our own simulation of the pool's level.

media.caption: The pool before (left, empty) and after (right): still water mirroring the openings above.
Crouched over the pool: the bright openings in the rock reflected in the water.
The zone map with its legend. Black: the sculpture's pillars and walls, where there is no floor (P1 to P10).

title: A floor lived in for years: a pool, moss where it is wet and shaded, bare stone under the drips (first pass)
notes: What would grow and live where on this floor, after years of the same rain and light? The floor was divided into zones from what was measured on the real sculpture: how much water reaches each spot (mostly running off the stone and dripping from its edges, very little straight from the sky), how much sun it gets over the day, how much sky it sees, and how much rock hangs over it. The surprise: wetness and sun hardly go together here, because most of the water comes off the rock, not through the openings where the sun comes in.

A pool: the natural hollow at the back of the floor is now a small pool, about 0.4 square metres and up to 12 cm deep, that can hold about 23 litres when full. Its shore follows the land: it was shaped the way a lake fills, from the lowest ground outward, and it is closed by a slight bank. It stays well away from the foot of the rock. Its bottom and margin are mud, and nothing roots in it.
Under the drips: where heavy drops hammer the floor, nothing rooted survives. Those lines are now bare, washed stone with small pebbles, and plants are thinned within a few centimetres of them.

Moss and grass by zone: moss now spreads as a carpet over the stone itself in the wet shade along the walls, and in patches in the half-light and at the pool's edge. Grass and the pale flowers grow where it is both wet and lit, and only in the cracks between the stones, no longer on top of them; the dry areas keep only a few tufts. In Gloam's violet light the moss reads dark olive rather than bright green.

A first pass, for review: the pool is shown empty, and the light on the floor around it was still the one computed for the old, flat floor when these were rendered. Next: the pool filling in the rain, muddy water that clears as it settles, and the small life of a floor like this (snails, woodlice, springtails, toads at the pool).
The new floor costs no extra drawing time: measured on the same views with and without it, the difference is within the run-to-run variation (slightly faster, with fewer blades of grass).
Offline renders, made frame by frame; not something you can walk through.
Sources: our own analysis of the light, sky and water maps measured on the sculpture; no published ecological model.

title: Falling drops: rounded streaks with a touch of lens
notes: Samuel found the falling drops looked like flat rectangular ribbons. Each drop is drawn as what the eye collects from it during one frame of a VR display (1/90 of a second): it moves several centimetres in that time, so it leaves a short streak.

Now each streak has the true shape of a moving sphere's trace: thickest through its middle, tapering at both ends, with nothing square about it. Close drops, wider than a pixel, show half of the water sphere's own image (its bright rim, the cave seen through it upside down) over half of the soft average glow the old strips had. The half-and-half mix is Samuel's artistic choice, between the soft strips and the full lens; the full lens and the first attempts are in the archive.
One more choice, not physics: a drop passing within 12 cm of the viewer's eyes is not drawn, because a drop that close would land on the viewer's face.
Real drops also wobble as they fall (from about 1 mm across), which would soften the bright rim further; that is not modelled until measured wobble sizes are found.
All offline renders, made frame by frame from the same storm and viewpoint; not something you can walk through.

Sources: Garg and Nayar 2003 (how a raindrop gathers light); Garg and Nayar 2006, Photorealistic rendering of rain streaks; Tokay and Beard 1996, field study of raindrop oscillations (oscillations begin at about 1 mm diameter); the refractive index of water and Fresnel's equations.

title: Flowers in the rain, breathing walls, and a walk over the living ground
notes: Plants: every plant now sways at its own pace (grass quick, flowers slower under their blooms; only the drifting gusts are shared), and dips and springs back when drops hit it.

Rain on the plants, in three steps. First a uniform test rate (heavier than the storm, to judge the dips). Then the storm's own drop landings near each plant, about 930 drops per square metre per second on average over the floor in the downpour (less than open sky, because the sculpture shelters most of the floor). Now the real thing: every falling drop is traced down its path, stops on the first bloom, stem or leaf it meets, and pushes that plant with its own momentum (its mass times its speed). In the first two minutes of the storm about 5,700 drops hit a plant, under 1 % of the drops that reach the floor.

Breathing architecture: the strand crests sway in a slow current, the tallest lobes move like anemones, and a breath travels across the walls. Shown at two strengths: subtle (crests a few millimetres, tall lobes about a centimetre) and twice that, to read the motion clearly. This motion is art-directed.
A walk through the cave over the living ground: broken stone with grass and flowers in the cracks.
Every clip is an offline render, made frame by frame; not something you can walk through.
Sources: Gunn and Kinzer 1949 (how fast drops fall, for their momentum). How stiff and heavy each plant is, and the walls' breathing, are estimates and artistic choices, not measured values.

media.caption: Plants hit by the storm's actual drops: each drop stops on the plant it meets and pushes it. Physical rain.
Dry: every plant at its own pace.
Test rain, heavier than the storm (1,500 drops per square metre per second everywhere), to judge the dips.
The step before: hits drawn at the rate of the storm's drops landing around each plant.
Breathing walls, subtle (art-directed).
Breathing walls, twice the amplitude (art-directed).
A walk through the cave over the living ground.

title: Where rain reaches the floor, and edges that obey their water supply
notes: A map of where rain actually reaches the ground under and around the sculpture, seen from above. Particles fall from a 1 cm grid over the whole site, run down the stone, drip off overhangs and edges, and land. The colour is how much water each spot receives compared with open sky: outside it is 1 (purple); under the stone most of the floor gets almost nothing (black), and the water arrives in bright rings and drip lines along the edges above, tens of times open-sky rain.

The inside floor (9 square metres, blue outline) receives the rain of about 13.6 square metres of sky, almost all of it (13.2) after running on the stone; only 0.4 comes straight through the openings in the roof. (The catchment map counts 14.4: the extra 0.8 lands on the floor outside first and runs in across it, which this map, made before that step, leaves out.) This map is now the input for a living ground: the floor under the sculpture shaped by where water has fallen for years.

Floor water, same day: a new test checks that a creeping puddle edge advances only as fast as water can reach it through the thin sheet behind it, as the physics of thin films requires. Edges were running 1.5 times too fast; two corrections bring them in line, and spreading puddles came out rounder too.

Known limits: the map ignores splash redistribution and soaking, and drips fall straight down (still air near the stone). Straight puddle edges still advance about 9 % slower in some directions than others; round puddles are round to 1 %.

Sources: Barnes, Lehman and Mulla 2014, priority-flood depression filling (Computers and Geosciences); Cox 1986 and Voinov 1976, contact-line speed (the Cox-Voinov law); Snoeijer and Eggers 2010, thin-film flow (Physical Review E).

media.caption: Water reaching the floor per unit of rain, top view, still air (log colour scale; 1 = open sky). Blue: the inside floor.

title: Thrown water settles: the same bucket, with the water surface lit, and a rebuilt splash model
notes: The same 10 litre bucket thrown along the floor, but drawn as light catching the water surface instead of colours for depth. Ripples show as light and shade; level water shows as even blue. Left: clean polished stainless steel. Right: limestone-like stone. Real time, 6 m floor, top view.

Why the change: the last video looked as if the water never finished settling. Measured, it does: inside the sheets the surface is flat to 0.02 mm at the 10 cm scale by 12 s, and a new test checks that a sheet levels at the rate the physics of a thin layer gives (within about 1 % of the exact solution). The blotches in the depth map were the floor's own 1 mm unevenness showing through level water.

Steel: how readily water lets go of stainless steel varies widely with how the surface was cleaned, polished and stored (the angle a retreating water edge makes with it ranges from 6 to 70 degrees across published measurements), so the steel is now named by its surface. This one is a laboratory-polished sample measured by Fu, Li and Fan 2024 (water meets it at 84 degrees as it advances and 49.5 degrees as it retreats). Thin film left behind on it now pulls back into the puddle or breaks up instead of staying stuck.

Splash: rebuilt from published measurements. Only the speed into the surface counts. Rough stone throws off far more of a raindrop's water as spray than smooth steel: about 23 % on stone, 7 % on brushed steel, 0.3 % on polished steel (from the splash counts and sizes of Stow and Hadfield and Stow and Stainer). Droplets keep part of a slanted drop's sideways speed, small drops bounce off water, and thrown lumps now splash a little (about 0.5 % of their water).

Known limits: how a thin film on steel breaks into puddles (the lace on the left) comes from a simplified rule that measures 0.4 to 0.9 times the right retreat speed; it will be rebuilt so the shape of the break-up is physical. Which steel the piece uses (clean or everyday) is still an open choice.

Sources: Bai, Rusche and Gosman 2002 and Rodrigues 2011 (splash regimes); Stow and Hadfield 1980 and Stow and Stainer 1977 (raindrop splash counts and sizes); Mundo, Sommerfeld and Tropea 1995 (oblique impact); Cossali, Coghe and Marengo 1997 (splash on films); Okawa et al. 2006 (splash on water); Brown, Jepsen and Yoon 2008 (large drops); Fu, Li and Fan 2024 (stainless steel contact angles); Lamb 1932 and Liu and Orfila 2004 (wave damping).

title: A 10 litre bucket thrown on steel and on stone (top view)
notes: A bucket thrown along the floor from the left edge: 10 L leave the hand in 0.3 s in a sweeping underarm swing at about 3 m/s, fly with air drag, and land as lumps plus a fringe of drops, about 1.4 m ahead. Left: stainless steel (a sink: it drinks nothing, and thin water on it breaks up). Right: limestone-like stone (it drinks). Real time, 6 m floor, seen straight from above.

This is the simulation's own data drawn as a map (blue = water depth, 0 to 5 mm), not a styled render, so the physics can be judged first. The thrown water keeps its forward speed: it sweeps on as a thin sheet at about 2 m/s, with streaks along the flow and crossing V-shaped waves (the oblique jumps a fast thin sheet makes). On steel the thinning tail breaks into dry holes and patches; on stone it stays a thin film that soaks in.

What changed since the last video: an audit found that every earlier 'thrown' bucket had silently lost all its forward momentum on landing (it landed as if dropped), that the floor's time stepping added energy to small waves, and several other bugs; each fix now has a test. The puddle edge now opens when the water's push (its speed as well as its height) beats surface tension.

Known limits: the first second is too blocky (a straight front and straight sides). A depth-averaged floor model has no rim instability of its own, so the irregular, fingered outline of a real throw can only come from how the lumps land; that, and the exact release of a real throw, wait for a filmed reference throw. About a third of the thin tail on steel can stay in cells not yet counted as part of the puddle (an open item).

title: One foot square of rain on stone: splash, puddles, ripples
notes: A test bench, before going back to the sculpture: heavy rain (100 mm/h) falls for two minutes on a one foot square in the middle of an 8 ft slab of limestone-like stone, nothing else in the scene. Real speed. Seen from 1, 3, 6 and 9 ft away, looking down at 45 degrees. No motion blur, no depth of field: every frame is an instant, drops at their real size.

What happens, and why. The square darkens within seconds: the stone drinks the first rain. Every drop throws a burst of tiny droplets (0.1 to 0.5 mm) that land up to 30-40 cm away, so a soft dark halo of splash grows around the square and fades out with distance. After about 20 seconds the stone's surface is full and water starts to stand; puddles join up and, once they meet stone that splash and wicking have already wetted, they spill past the square in rounded lobes (by 2:00, about 660 cm2 of standing water outside the square). Water also creeps sideways inside the stone, slowly: a few millimetres in two minutes, about 3 cm in an hour.

On the standing water: rings travel out from each impact, cross, bounce off the puddle edges and fade. They are real height, a tenth of a millimetre, so they read faintly. The small clear circles are falling drops; the brief vertical streaks under some of them are their reflections, stretched by the ripples (the way moonlight stretches on rippled water).

Physics, briefly: absorption at the rate measured for limestone (Hall and Hoff), puddle edges held by surface tension on dry stone (about 2.2 mm high) and feathering onto wet stone, splash counts, sizes, speeds and angles from published drop-impact studies (Stow and Hadfield 1980, Stow and Stainer 1977, Mundo, Sommerfeld and Tropea 1995), a water balance that accounts for every drop. The simulation was independently reviewed before this render, and every finding was fixed.
Known limits: no evaporation yet (damp stone never dries); the stone has no colour texture, so the look is plain; ripples in deep water fade a little slower than they should.

media.caption: The same two minutes from 1, 3, 6 and 9 ft away.
1 ft away, full frame: puddle edges, splash droplets, falling drops, ripples.

superseded_note: Rendered with the first floor model. It was then checked and rebuilt with a standard method from hydraulic engineering: small waves no longer gain energy (so puddles settle), puddle edges were corrected, and thrown water keeps its momentum. The next study tested the rebuilt model with a thrown bucket.

title: Where the rain goes: a map of the sky above the sculpture
notes: Which rain ends up inside? To answer it once and for all, 650,000 particles were dropped from above the sculpture, about one per square centimetre over the whole site. Each falls, runs downhill along the stone wherever it lands, drips off overhangs, spills over ledges, and is followed until it reaches the ground.

Every square of sky is then coloured by where its water ends up. In still air, rain falling on about 14.4 square metres of sky ends up on the 9 square metres of floor inside. Only 0.4 square metres of it falls straight through the openings without touching stone: most finds its way in by running down the inner walls, along the tubes that reach far out from the building, and through the low openings at the floor. A little more (0.8 square metres) lands on the floor outside and then runs or spills in across it, filling low spots on the way like real puddles.

In a light wind (2 m/s) the rain slants. The openings are tall, narrow shafts, so slanted rain hits their walls instead of falling through: the straight-through share drops to 0.14 square metres, while the water that runs in along the stone stays about the same.
This map now decides where rain is simulated in detail for the views from inside.
Sources: Barnes, Lehman and Mulla 2014, priority-flood depression filling (Computers and Geosciences), for how water fills low spots and spills over.

media.caption: Still air. Left: the sky above the site (colour key below), each centimetre coloured by where its rain ends up: blue falls straight onto the inside floor, cyan reaches the inside floor after running down the stone, green lands on the floor outside and then runs or spills inside, grey ends up on the ground outside. The black outline is the floor inside the sculpture. Right: where that water arrives on the inside floor, darker where more arrives.

The routes of forty sampled particles that end up inside. Black dots are where they start above the sculpture, red crosses where they reach the floor. Some start well outside the floor area and run in along the tubes. Right: their height along the way.

title: An eight-minute storm: the stone fills, runs, and pools at its feet
notes: Limestone drinks. In a short storm it soaks up most of the rain and only darkens; it has to fill before it sheds. So this storm runs eight minutes: one of drizzle, two of rain, five of downpour, with a gusty wind.

By the end the walls are saturated and running, water braids down the folds of the sculpture, and at the foot of a wall it has collected into a puddle on the concrete floor. Some of it has drained out past the edge of the floor onto the ground outside.

The physics behind it: drop sizes and fall speeds from rain measurements, drops that bead, creep, slide and merge, splash spray that shakes resting drops loose, stone that takes water up and dries the way porous stone does, and a floor that collects, soaks and drains.

media.caption: Ten seconds in real time, near the end of the downpour, inside the tube: drops slide down the channels and fresh water glints where it is running.

title: Rain seen from inside: stains in the stone, the floor junction, looking out
notes: Everything is now seen from inside, as the visitor always is. A 3-minute storm (drizzle, rain, downpour) with a gusty 2 m/s wind, on limestone walls, a slightly porous concrete box top and earth around it.

The traces are painted into the stone itself: the surface around each shot is subdivided to about 3 mm and every recorded path and impact wets it with a soft falloff. No more ribbons floating on or sinking into the surface. Gloss only where water is running now; dark stain where it has been.

Before these renders, an independent review of the simulation checked it against the physics literature; its corrections are in: drips now let go at their real size, drops slide at speeds that depend on their size, and water flows from surface to surface instead of piling up. Detail is spent where a visitor inside can see it, from crawling to standing height.

title: Rain on limestone: a 3-minute storm, wet traces, films and channels
notes: Our own GPU rain solver, rendered in clay: grey stone, blue water. The drops started as spheres (ping pong balls), became teardrops, and are now sessile drops that have wet the stone: flat base on the rock, edge feathering into it, full downhill and thin uphill, in the rounded, corner and cusp shapes running drops take.

The rock now remembers water. A sliding drop leaves a film behind; later drops grip less on wet stone, run faster, and steer toward wetter rock beside them, so they get captured by earlier paths. On the upper surfaces the tracks branch and converge into channels on their own.
On wet rock, water joins a film instead of beading. Excess film is held until there is enough to let go as a new drop (the bathtub micro-dam), which is also where drips under overhangs now come from.
What you see as a trace is drawn from the exact recorded path of every drop, snapped onto the stone, not from the coarse per-face map the physics uses.

The stone is limestone (~8% porosity). A storm from dry rock: a minute of drizzle, a minute of rain, a minute of downpour. On limestone a fresh trail is glossy for about a second, then soaks in and stays as a dark stain for hours: the stain is the trace of where water has been. Drops spread on soaked stone instead of beading. Next: the floor as a real destination for the water, and proper water shading.

title: A custom real-time player for Gloam
notes: Gloam's day of light is about 16,000 lightmaps (pictures of the light on every surface, each 8K) that must stream in while the visitor walks. In the Unity version, every change of lightmap pauses the program for 80 to 95 thousandths of a second, which is the source of the stutter, the limit on how fast the day can play and the loading indicator. To remove that limit at its root, we started a custom real-time player for Gloam, written from scratch.

First measurements on a workstation, rendering the full sculpture (5.9 million triangles) for two eyes at a current headset's resolution (about 2K per eye): about 4 thousandths of a second of graphics-card time per picture. A headset shows 90 pictures a second, so each must be ready in 11.1 thousandths of a second; none came close to that limit, even while loading lightmaps back to back at more than ten times Unity's maximum rate.
Known limits: measured on a workstation, without a headset.
Sources: measurements on our own workstation; no outside source.

media.caption: Frame 640 of the day, rendered by the new player from where the visitor starts.

title: Re-baking the light: a first test against Octane
notes: The original lightmaps took about a year of overnight rendering in Octane (around 3 minutes per 8K map at the end). We tested whether modern GPU ray tracing can produce the same light much faster. Reading the original Octane project revealed that the sculpture's material is a plain grey: all of Gloam's purple comes from the light itself, a blue sky and blue ground mixing with a red sunset.

A first test bake of the main interior piece, using the same material and sky colours, took 4.6 seconds at 2K resolution (about 75 seconds at the full 8K, before any denoising) and places the light where Octane did (0.92 correlation). Colours are not yet a match: the upper wall reads redder than Octane's blue-violet, because Octane's sky model is not public and is approximated here.

We also measured how the bounced light changes as the sun moves: smoothly enough that a handful of snapshots per hour of the day, blended, reproduce the in-between moments within 1.5 %. That points to a live version of Gloam's light: sharp sunlight and shadows computed in real time, soft bounced light precomputed, so clouds, weather and passing birds can change the light as you watch.
Known limits: one piece of the sculpture, one moment of the day, noisy, and the sky colours are still approximate.

media.caption: Left, the original Octane lightmaps. Right, the same view with the main interior piece re-baked on the GPU in seconds.

superseded_note: Rewritten for a general audience the same morning, with the main finding first: the light can be computed far faster and lands in the right places, but its colour does not yet match Octane's sky.

title: Can the light be made faster? Not yet in colour
notes: The question. All of Gloam's colour is light. The sculpture itself is plain grey; the purples, blues and reds come from a simulated sky that changes from dawn to dusk. Octane needed about a year of overnight rendering to capture that day as 16,000 lightmaps. We tested whether a modern graphics card could compute the same light in seconds, and one day perhaps live.

What works. A first test computed the light on the main interior piece in a few seconds instead of minutes. The light lands in the right places: the bright patches, the dark folds and the glow around the openings match Octane's.

What does not work yet: the colour. Octane's sky is more than a blue dome with a sun. Through the day it shifts between deep blue, violet and the red of the low sun, and those tints mix differently in every fold of the sculpture. Our test sky is a simple approximation, so it gives one flat mood: next to Octane, the walls look too warm and too uniform, and the subtle blue-to-violet gradients are missing. Matching that sky, at every hour of the day, is the main open problem. Until it is solved, the player keeps Octane's original lightmaps for the artwork; the faster light is used only for tests (some rain clips show it, labelled).

Why it is still worth pursuing. We also measured how the soft, bounced light changes as the sun moves. It changes slowly and smoothly, so a few snapshots per hour of the day can be blended to recreate any moment in between. If the sky colour can be matched, only the sharp sunlight would need to be computed live. Weather, clouds and the shadows of passing birds could then change the light as you watch.
Limits: one piece of the sculpture, one moment of the day, a simplified sky.
Sources: Kajiya 1986, The rendering equation (the physics both Octane and our test compute).

media.caption: Left, Octane's original light. Right, our fast test on the main interior piece. The light falls in the same places, but the colour is flatter and warmer than Octane's sky.

Two things improved: grains now land on the true surface of the sculpture instead of an approximation a few centimetres above it, and each grain's sunlight is computed against the real sculpture on every frame of the day, not just at one baked moment.
The image shows the check that the light is right: grains in sunlight (red) sit exactly in the sun patch on the floor, grains in shade are blue.
Known limits: at the current art-directed values the motes are very sparse in still images; they need to be judged in motion, in the headset.

title: The dust in the sunbeams
notes: What you see. In Gloam, tiny specks of dust drift through the air. Most of the time they are almost invisible. When they cross a ray of sun coming through an opening, they light up, and that is what makes the sunbeams visible. Some settle on the rock and floor, and gusts of wind lift them again.

What changed. The dust now runs inside the new player instead of Unity. It keeps the look that was already settled. Two things are better: the grains settle on the real surface of the sculpture, not slightly above it; and each grain knows at every moment whether the sun can reach it, so the beams move correctly through the whole day, not only at one baked moment. So far it has been tried on a workstation only.

How we checked it. The image is a test view, not the artwork. Every grain is drawn large: red where the sun reaches it, blue in shadow. The red ones sit only on the patches of sun on the floor, so the beams are in the right place.
Limits: dust is about movement and is very sparse in a still image. It has to be judged in motion. The amount and size of the dust are art-directed.

title: What a visitor can actually see
notes: We simulated about 50,000 positions a curious visitor's head can reach inside the cave, most of them only by leaning in: standing, crouching, lying on the floor looking up, putting their head into the tubes, looking in every direction. About 80 % of the sculpture's surface (some 380 square metres of stone in all) is seen from somewhere inside; the remaining fifth (hidden folds, the exterior) never is. And 182 square metres, about half of the stone, can be seen from closer than 25 cm, by visitors who crouch, lie down and press their faces to the rock.

This explains why pixels can show in the current build: uniform 8K maps spend most of their detail on surfaces nobody sees and too little on the ones people press close to. The new lighting direction puts detail only where it can be seen, at the density each surface needs.

Correction: an earlier version of this entry said 59 % of the surface was never seen. It placed visitors' heads only on a grid over the open floor and missed everything a visitor sees by leaning into the tubes or lying under an overhang (Samuel caught it). The corrected figure is about 20 %, and the area seen from closer than 25 cm went from 44 to 182 square metres. The first figure is kept in the archive.
Method: our own measurement, rays traced from each head position against the full sculpture; no outside source.

title: A living ground
notes: Until now the floor under the sculpture was flat and dead. We are giving it a history: what this ground would look like if the space had stood for years under real rain, wind and time. The shaping is grounded in the sculpture itself: how much rain reaches each part of the floor (mostly dripping and running off the stone, from the rain research's floor-arrival map, second image), how much sky and sun each spot gets over the day, and where the rock meets the floor.

A first simulated history gives about 15 cm of relief: hollows and channels under the drip lines, mud where water lingers, sand and dust in dry corners, stones laid bare where water ran. The ground never drops where the sculpture meets it, so no new openings appear at its base. Next: building it in 3D with grass, moss, stones and a few strange flowers where life would take hold, and possibly a scent for each part of the ground.
Known limits: a first pass, shown from above; the plant growth rules still need work.
Sources: our own simplified simulation of years of weather (where drips fall, erosion and deposition season by season, slopes slumping, stones resisting), not a published erosion model.

media.caption: First simulated history of the floor, from above: materials (left), relief (middle, blue = hollows), where water flows (right).

title: How wet stone and rain really look: what the research says
notes: Before drawing any water in Gloam's own player, we read what science has measured about how wet things look, and it corrected several of our own assumptions.

Stone darkens when wet for two reasons: light gets trapped under the thin film of water and has more chances to be absorbed, and water filling the pores makes the stone scatter less light. A surprise: pale stone darkens less than dark stone, in proportion. Pale carbonate sand loses only about a tenth of its brightness when wet (Zhang and Voss); the figure's model curve for a pale stone gives a sixth. So a pale cave will not turn dramatically dark in rain; a photograph of the real stone, dry and wet, will set the exact amount.

A falling raindrop is a tiny lens: it gathers light from a wide cone of the scene behind it, so it usually looks brighter than its background, whatever that background is. A VR display has no motion blur, and a drop drawn once per frame at 90 frames per second would appear as a string of separate dots about 10 cm apart. What the eye sees in reality is closer to a faint streak, so the drops are drawn as the streak the eye collects during one frame. Drips inside the cave fall more slowly than rain from the sky (4 to 8 m/s instead of about 9).

Over the life of an exhibition, the visible record of the weather will come from dust, the channels rain washes through it, faint rings where puddles dry, and drying stains. Rain cleans dust realistically: partly, more where drops strike, never completely. Mineral growth on the stone itself is far too slow to see (microns per week).

Sources: Lekner and Dorf 1988 (why things are darker when wet); Twomey, Bohren and Mergenthaler 1986 (pore filling); Jensen, Legakis and Dorsey 1999 (rendering wet materials); Zhang and Voss 2006 (wet carbonate sand); Garg and Nayar 2003 and 2006 (appearance of raindrops and rain streaks); Sartor and Boyd 1972 (street dust wash-off); Righetti and Lucarelli 2007 (detachment by drop impact); Deegan et al. 1997, Hu and Larson 2002, Popov 2005 (rings left by drying drops); Lienhard (heat and mass transfer, drying); Dreybrodt 1999 and Baker 1998 (calcite growth rates).

media.caption: Left: how much darker stones of different tones get when wet; pale stone keeps most of its brightness. Right: why a falling drop is hard to show on a VR display: drawn once per frame it becomes a string of dots, while the eye sees a faint streak.

title: The rain study moves into Gloam's own player
notes: Until now, every picture of the rain studies was made in Blender, on a plain grey floor under a generic sky. Today the same simulation, a square foot of rain falling on stone, was drawn for the first time by Gloam's own player, inside the cave, on the cave floor, in the cave's own light.

These are offline renders, made one frame at a time from a fixed viewpoint, so they can be compared picture by picture with the earlier ones. They are a check, not the artwork, and not yet something you can walk through.

The comparison passes where it matters. The wet square sits in exactly the same place, and the scattered stains of the first seconds of rain appear in the same pattern at the same moment. So the player reads the simulation faithfully.

The wet stone is much less dark than in Blender, on purpose. The Blender version used a hand-chosen dark colour. The player follows the physics of why things look darker when wet, and a pale stone like Gloam's floor darkens only a little. The real amount will be set from a photograph of the actual stone, dry and wet.
Next: the water's own reflections of the cave, then the falling drops and splashes.
Sources: Lekner and Dorf 1988 (why some things are darker when wet).

title: Sunbeams made of dust
notes: A sunbeam in a dusty room is millions of grains, each too small to see, catching the light together. Gloam's player now shows that: beams of glowing dust cross the cave from the openings to the patches of sun on the rock and floor. The beams are not painted. They are dust drifting in the cave's wind, and they glow only where the sun really reaches through the sculpture, so their edges are the edges of the openings and they move as the day moves.

The dust also takes its colour from Gloam's own light. In the beams it has the tint of the sunlit patches; in the shade, grains catch the purple and blue glow of the cave around them, so dust is faintly there everywhere, not only in the sun.
Limits: a first pass, judged on a monitor; the amount and size of the dust are art-directed. Dust is about movement and depth, and has to be judged in motion.
Sources: ported from the artist's own dust system in Unity and tuned by eye; no published model.

A still from the same place.

title: Rain over the whole cave floor
notes: The earlier rain studies fell on a single square foot, by design, to check the physics. Now the rain falls over the entire floor of the cave, on the new living ground of broken stone plates, and only the water the sky actually delivers reaches it, directly or off the stone.

Most of the water does not fall straight in. The sculpture is mostly closed above, so rain first lands on the stone, runs down it and drips off its edges onto the floor. Our earlier map of where the sky's water goes decides where every drop and every drip arrives.

On the ground the water does what water does: it soaks into the stone, darkens it, fills the cracks between the plates first, then gathers into shallow puddles, two to three millimetres deep, in the hollows. Outside the walls it runs off in channels across the sand. The images follow a two and a half minute storm that goes from drizzle to heavy rain.

Seen from inside, in Gloam's own player, the stone darkens where it is wet, by the measured amount for pale stone, and the puddles reflect the lit cave around them. These are offline renders, made frame by frame, not yet something you can walk through.

An honest finding about rain itself: in a dim cave, real raindrops are almost invisible. Each drop is a tiny lens that crosses any point in a few thousandths of a second. We render the physical version first, and separately a clearly labelled heightened version, so the choice of how visible the rain should be is an artistic one, made with eyes open.

Making the physics hold took a finer grid than the ground itself: the water is simulated on 4 mm cells, because coarser cells failed our own checks (water sheeting down a slope came out half as deep as it should).

Since the first clips (kept in the archive), which looked more like a video game than like rain: every drop that lands in a puddle now sends out rings that travel at the measured speed of small water waves, bounce off the puddle's edge and fade, so the reflections shimmer and break up; edges are smoothed; and a bug that lost about a third of the water running off the stone is fixed. In the clips with the original light, puddle edges also fade where the film thins below the stone's grain, and each drop is drawn at its true size; the two clips with the test light are from just before that step.

Sources: Marshall and Palmer 1948 (raindrop sizes); Gunn and Kinzer 1949 (falling speeds); Stow and Hadfield 1980, Mundo et al. 1995 (splash); Lekner and Dorf 1988 (why things look darker when wet); Garg and Nayar 2003 (how a raindrop gathers light).

title: Falling drops: flat strips against water spheres, first two attempts
notes: Samuel found the falling drops looked like flat rectangular ribbons. Each drop is drawn as what the eye collects from it during one frame of a VR display (1/90 of a second): it moves several centimetres in that time, so it leaves a short streak. The old version drew that streak as a flat strip of one colour.

First attempt: the true trace of a moving sphere, thickest through its middle and tapering at both ends, with drops wider than a pixel drawn as tiny lenses, each point showing the cave reflected off the water and seen through it upside down. Close drops came out as two thin bright lines with broken dashes between them, which read worse than the old strips.

Second attempt: each pixel averaged the drop over its own width, a sampling mistake that painted the edge of the drop as its brightest part was fixed, and drops passing within 12 cm of the viewer's eyes were no longer drawn (a drop that close would land on the viewer's face). The two bright lines stayed: a water sphere in a dark cave with a few bright openings shows a thin bright ring, and a falling drop sweeps that ring into two lines.
All offline renders, made frame by frame from the same storm and viewpoint; not something you can walk through.

Sources: Garg and Nayar 2003 (a raindrop gathers light from a 165 degree field of view); Garg and Nayar 2006, Photorealistic rendering of rain streaks; the refractive index of water (1.333) and Fresnel's equations for reflection at a water surface.
